name: Ak-Say Valley
near: There are practically no permanent villages in the valley — in summer there are yak herders’ camps, border posts and hunting bases. Entry is via the Kyndy pass (3,400 m) and the border post south of the At-Bashy range; the nearest large settlement with services is At-Bashy, the town of Naryn is about 120 km of gravel from the valley (NomadCar). The earlier “1 Maya ~34 km” is an OSM point in a straight line across the range, not a guide for travel.
elev: About 3,000–3,100 m (Trip to Kyrgyzstan, Baibol — 3,000 m; Nomad's Land — 3,100 m; map.kg — “above 3,000 m”).
short: Ak-Say is a huge high-altitude (≈3,000–3,100 m) treeless valley between the At-Bashy range and Kakshaal-Too on the border with China, Kyrgyzstan’s “cold pole” (−56.3 °C) and the way to Lake Kel-Suu.
desc: The valley stretches for about 100 km, up to 40 km wide (Nomad's Land), south of the At-Bashy range as far as the Kakshaal-Too range, along which runs the border with China. The absolute minimum temperature in Kyrgyzstan was recorded here — −56.3 °C; because of the harsh climate only low grasses and rare shrubs grow, there are no trees, and there are small lakes and marshes. Ak-Say is a key biodiversity area (KGZ24, ~90,000 ha): Marco Polo argali, snow leopard, ibex, wolf, marmot, demoiselle crane; 93 glaciers in the Aksai river basin with an area of 120.9 km². In summer yak herders come up here, and some stay with their yaks in winter too. There is a Neolithic site in the valley, hunting bases operate, and mountains up to 6,000 m attract climbers. The road to the Kok-Kyya valley and Lake Kel-Suu passes through Ak-Say; the whole valley is a border zone with a mandatory permit.
guide: Ak-Say is a vastness you will not see anywhere else in Kyrgyzstan: after the Kyndy pass the road comes out onto a flat steppe up to 40 km wide, and to the south the Kakshaal-Too stands like a wall with the Chinese border. Look around — argali, marmots and demoiselle cranes live here, and yaks graze by the road. Remember that this is the country’s “cold pole”: even in July there can be sub-zero temperatures at night, so keep warm things at hand. Most people drive through the valley in transit to Kel-Suu — ask the driver to stop for a couple of photo breaks at the small lakes and on the climb to Kyndy. You cannot get here without a permit, so arrange it in advance.
see: A steppe valley up to 40 km wide and a panorama of the Kakshaal-Too range (the Chinese border); the Kyndy pass (3,400 m) at the entrance; wildlife — argali, marmots, demoiselle cranes; herds of yaks and summer camps; small lakes and marshes; the descent into the Kok-Kyya canyon.
skip: You are not going to Kel-Suu or on an expedition — it makes little sense to arrange a permit and drive 120+ km on gravel for the valley itself. You want forests and warm nights: here is a treeless steppe and a “cold pole”. You do not have a prepared 4×4.
diff: Moderate-high — because of the road: washboard gravel, dust, vibration, risk of punctures (NomadCar); altitude 3,000–3,400 m; the valley itself has no trails or infrastructure.
when: July — August (warm, the road is dry, the Kok-Kyya camps operate). In June snow is possible, from September frosts; in winter down to −40…−56 °C, snow up to 80 cm — trips are not recommended.
hours: An open border area — only with a border permit, checked at the post after the Kyndy pass. Hunting bases operate seasonally, hunting is by licence (Baibol). Since 10.04.2026 permanent residents working on the Ak-Say and Arpa pastures pass without a permit or fee according to lists from the ayil kenesh (village councils) (time.kg); this does not apply to tourists.
daytime: Daytime: plan to cross the valley in daylight to reach the Kok-Kyya camp by evening; morning and evening have the best light and animal activity (editorial).
how: Bishkek → Naryn (≈350 km, paved) → At-Bashy → the Kyndy pass (3,400 m) and the border post → Ak-Say valley. From Naryn to the valley it is about 120 km of gravel (NomadCar), then 60–80 km to Kok-Kyya.
needcar: Yes, a 4×4 with a local driver; there is no public transport.
self: Only with a border permit (CBT Naryn, tour.too.kg) and in a prepared 4×4; not recommended without a local driver.
roadtype: Gravel/dirt with washboard and dust (NomadCar); the Kyndy pass 3,400 m; the At-Bashy — Kyndy — Torugart road was graded in August 2026 (time.kg); in the valley — rutted dirt tracks and swampy sections.
traveltime: Bishkek — Naryn ~5–6 h; Naryn — Ak-Say valley ~3–4 h on gravel (calculated: ~120 km at 30–40 km/h, NomadCar); from Almaty to Ak-Say — 15–16 h (Freedom Travel, 07.2025).
stay: There are no tourist hotels in the valley itself; there are hunting bases (by arrangement) and tents. People usually stay overnight in yurt camps in the Kok-Kyya valley (Kel-Suu Yurt Camp — from 1,800 som per 2GIS; 1,500–2,500+ som per person with meals — kgnomad 2026) or in Naryn/At-Bashy.
net: There is no mobile coverage after leaving Naryn/the last villages; a weak signal is occasionally found on the passes (NomadCar, kgnomad 2026).
entry: There is no fee to visit the valley; a border permit is mandatory: CBT Naryn — €30 (Naryn region, one week), €35 (several regions), €50 urgent; tour.too.kg — 3,000 som (2026). Hunting — by separate licences.
transfer: 4×4 Naryn — Kok-Kyya (via Ak-Say) — Naryn: 13,000–20,000+ som per car for up to 4 people (kgnomad, 07.2026). Marshrutka (minibus) Bishkek — Naryn — 600 som (CBT Naryn, 05.2026).
bring: Permit and passport; very warm clothing even in summer, hat and gloves; sunscreen and sunglasses; a supply of water and food (no shops); cash; a spare tyre and tools for the car; binoculars for watching animals.
warn: Border zone: a mandatory permit, do not drive towards the border and do not photograph the border posts. A “cold pole” — sharp temperature swings, snow is possible in summer. Altitude 3,000–3,400 m. No phone coverage, medical help or fuel — a full tank from Naryn/At-Bashy. Gravel washboard — frequent punctures.
food: There are no eateries in the valley. At the yak herders’ and in the Kok-Kyya camps — dairy products, kaymak, boorsok, beshbarmak (editorial). Stock up on food in Naryn.
reviews: No separate listings with ratings found on Google Maps (search is ambiguous, 03.10.2026) or TripAdvisor. In travellers’ reports (Freedom Travel 2025, TripAdvisor on Kel-Suu) the road through Ak-Say is called one of the most beautiful parts of the trip; cons — a bumpy gravel road and cold.
p.sum: Ak-Say is a huge high-altitude valley beyond the Kyndy pass (≈3,400 m), the “cold pole” of Kyrgyzstan; tourists drive through it on the way to Kok-Kyya and Kel-Suu. A border permit (checked at the posts at the entrance) and a 4×4 are needed: from Naryn ≈120 km of gravel, 3–4 h. There is no infrastructure — people overnight in the Kok-Kyya yurt camps or in At-Bashy/Naryn; bring a full tank, cash and food from Naryn.

p.permits: A border permit is mandatory (the border zone of the At-Bashy district by the Chinese border). Ways to arrange it: 1) tour.too.kg — 3,000 som (all border zones) / $35 for the Kel-Suu—Kok-Kyya—Chatyr-Kol zone; 5–7 working days; office at 105/3 Isanov St., Bishkek (2026). 2) CBT Naryn — €30 (Naryn region only, ~1 week), €35 (several regions), €50 urgent in 2 working days (stage 1); Nomad's Land: from Naryn fastest — within a few days, via Bishkek — up to 2 weeks. Step by step: (1) send a passport scan and travel dates (WhatsApp/form); (2) pay a 50% prepayment; (3) the Border Service reviews it for ~1 week; (4) pick up the paper original in Bishkek or Naryn (or via the guide/tour — then the passport copy is sent a few days ahead). The permit is valid for up to 1 month. It is checked at the military posts at the Kyndy pass/at the entrance to the Ak-Say valley (2 posts per Eurasia Travel) — you need the original permit with the stamp and your passport. Photographing the posts is prohibited. No fee for entry to the lake/valley was found. Hunting — by separate licences.
p.access: By car only: with children and older people — possible as part of a Kel-Suu trip if they tolerate the altitude of 3,000–3,400 m and the bumps well; in a wheelchair — only from the car window; with a dog — not advisable.
